primary_meaning: The metals in Nebuchadnezzar’s image symbolize a succession of earthly kingdoms or world empires. Their changing materials portray successive stages of imperial rule, culminating in a divided and unstable kingdom represented by iron mixed with clay; all are ultimately displaced by God’s everlasting kingdom.
primary_basis: Daniel 2:31–35 describes the image: a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze (“brass” in older translations), legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with clay.
Daniel 2:36–45 explicitly interprets the image as a sequence of kingdoms, beginning with Nebuchadnezzar’s Babylon as the head of gold and ending with God’s indestructible kingdom.
Daniel 7:1–27 is commonly treated as a parallel vision of four successive kingdoms followed by divine rule.
Daniel 8:3–25, especially 8:20–21, explicitly identifies Medo-Persia and Greece and is often used to clarify the historical sequence.
Revelation 13 and 17 are sometimes connected typologically or eschatologically with Daniel’s sequence of beastly empires.

alternatives.meaning: Traditional Christian identification: gold is Babylon, silver is Medo-Persia, bronze is Greece, iron is Rome, and the iron-and-clay phase represents Rome’s divided continuation, successor states, or a final revived form of Roman power.
basis: The longstanding Jewish and Christian four-empires scheme

alternatives.meaning: A widespread critical-historical identification: gold is Babylon, silver is Media, bronze is Persia, and iron is the Greek or Hellenistic empire; the iron-and-clay division reflects the fragmented successor kingdoms, often especially the Seleucid and Ptolemaic realms.
basis: The historical setting commonly assigned to Daniel by critical scholarship

alternatives.meaning: Dispensational-futurist reading: the feet and toes of iron mixed with clay symbolize an end-time confederation or revived Roman Empire immediately preceding Christ’s kingdom.

Idealist or typological reading: the metals represent the recurring character of human political power rather than a strictly exhaustive historical timetable; earthly empires are impressive but internally fragile and destined to yield to God’s reign.
basis: The contrast between the human-made image and the divinely established stone/kingdom

alternatives.meaning: Moralized readings in which the metals primarily symbolize declining human character, spiritual qualities, historical ages, or parts of an individual person.
basis: Analogical associations attached to the relative value or strength of the materials rather than Daniel’s explicit interpretation

notes: There is strong consensus on the basic meaning because Daniel 2 itself interprets the metals as successive kingdoms. There is no complete consensus on the precise identification of every kingdom or on whether the iron-and-clay stage is ancient, post-Roman, or future. The canonical image also includes iron, although the supplied term lists only gold, silver, brass/bronze, and clay.
